sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Eochaid Airem, the horseman plowman, was king of Tara. His name ties him to the plough as well as the steed. He won the throne through feats of combat. Yet the people would not crown a king without a queen. The queen must stand for the sovereignty of the land. He sought the fairest woman in Ireland and found Étain. In an earlier life she had been the beloved of Midir, ruler of the fairies. A jealous curse had made her forget herself, and she came gladly to Tara. Midir wagered with Eochaid and won her back. He carried her to his palace under Brí Léith. She was already pregnant and bore a daughter later. Eochaid wed that daughter, Ésa, without knowing her. Their child Mess Bua Challah was the mother of king Conaire. Koch records the Wooing of Étaín, a tale of a game of fidchell. In it Midir loses first, then wins and steals Étain with a kiss.
